{"stdout":"# Editorial playbook — AI Edge Briefing

You are producing today's edition of a daily briefing on frontier AI. The reader uses this as their single place to stay at the edge: the advances, the research, and how AI is being used for good and for harm — cyber, influence ops, military, health, science, policy. It is not a "fun uses of AI" newsletter. It is raw, factual, sourced.

The reader's standard: **every claim links to where it came from, every number is the number in the source, and nothing is written that the sources do not say.** If you cannot source it, it does not go in.

## 0. Setup

1. Work in the repo root. Determine today's date in **America/Toronto**: `TZ=America/Toronto date +%F`. That is the edition date, `DATE`.
2. `ls data/` — the previous edition tells you the cutoff. The coverage window (`WINDOW`) is from the previous edition's `generated_at` to now (if there is no previous edition, the 24 hours before now). Write it down as absolute timestamps in both UTC and ET; you will hand it to the subagents. Read the previous edition so you do not repeat it; a story already covered goes in again **only if there is a new development**, flagged `update`, and the bullets report only the new facts.
3. `node scripts/build.js --topics` — the existing topic slugs. Reuse them; only coin a new slug when nothing fits.
   `node scripts/build.js --storylines` — the open storylines (id, status, name, frame). An item that is a development in one of those arcs is **filed under it** (see §3, `storylines`). The daily never creates a storyline; the Monday Week in Review does.
4. Every day is a daily edition, Mondays included. The week in review is a separate weekly edition with its own playbook (`PROMPT-WEEK.md`) and its own routine — never part of the daily file.

## 0b. Keep your own context small — it is most of what this edition costs

Every turn you take re-sends this whole conversation. So the price of anything you pull into your context
is its size **times the number of turns that come after it** — a page you open early is paid for a hundred
times over. Measured: writing the edition costs about $3; re-reading the conversation while writing it costs
about $20. None of the rules below cost you a source, a check or an item. They stop you paying rent on text
you have already used.

1. **Write files with `Write`, and change them with `Edit`.** Never `cat > file <<'EOF'`, and never a
   `python3 -`/`node -e` script that does find-and-replace on a data file — those put the whole file, or
   whole paragraphs twice over, into the conversation as a command argument. `Edit` sends only the line that
   changes.
2. **Never print a file back out after writing it.** You know what you wrote. To check it, run the
   validator — it prints errors, not contents.
3. **Read the part you need.** `sed -n '40,80p'` over `cat` for anything long, and don't re-read a file
   that has not changed since you read it.
4. **`node scripts/fetch.js` caps its output at 12,000 characters** — the claim, the date and the figures
   are at the top of a page. Add `--full` only when you have looked and what you need is genuinely further
   down. Don't pipe it through `head` as well; the cap is already there.
5. **Let the subagents hold the raw material.** A beat opens fifty pages and hands you back a page of facts;
   that is the whole point of them. When you need a page opened and checked, and a subagent can do it,
   prefer that to opening it yourself.
6. Same rules for the subagents you launch — put a short version of this in every prompt you give them.

None of this licenses checking less. If a fact needs a source opened, open it. Verify everything §2 says to
verify. This is about what you keep afterwards, not what you look at.

## 1. Sweep the sources — four beats in parallel

Read `SOURCES.md`. Then launch **four general-purpose subagents in one message** with the Agent tool, one per beat. Give each: the `WINDOW` as absolute timestamps, its beat's source list from `SOURCES.md`, the **Sourcing rules** below verbatim, and the return format. Tell each to run many searches (15–30) and to open the listed primary sources directly. If the Agent tool is unavailable, work the four beats yourself in turn — do not skip any.

- **Beat A — Frontier models & labs · Compute, chips & infrastructure · Deployment & impact (industry, funding, labor).** SOURCES.md §1, §7, §8.
- **Beat B — Research & papers (incl. safety, alignment, evals).** SOURCES.md §2. arXiv new listings (cs.AI, cs.LG, cs.CL, cs.CR, cs.CV, cs.RO), Hugging Face papers, alphaXiv, Nature/Science, lab research blogs, Epoch, METR, AISI, CAISI, Apollo, Redwood, Alignment Forum. Prefer papers with a notable quantitative result, from major labs/universities, or drawing significant attention. Return arXiv IDs and author institutions.
- **Beat C — Security, misuse & threat intelligence · Military, defense & geopolitics.** SOURCES.md §3, §4. AI-enabled intrusions and malware, fraud and scams, deepfakes, influence operations, surveillance, prompt injection and agent exploits, model theft / illicit distillation, bio/chem misuse reports; procurement, deployment, autonomous weapons, export controls, national strategies.
- **Beat D — Health, science & medicine · Policy, regulation & law.** SOURCES.md §5, §6. Clinical results, FDA/Health Canada/WHO actions, drug discovery, AI for science, biosecurity; legislation, regulation, enforcement, court rulings and filings, government reports, standards — US federal and state, EU, UK, Canada, China, international bodies.

**Subagent return format** — one block per item, then a short list of rejected candidates and why:

```
SECTION: <one of the eight section names>
HEADLINE: <factual, specific, max 18 words, no hype>
PUBLISHED: <date/time and timezone exactly as the source shows it>
SOURCES: one per line — <publisher> | <exact URL> | primary or report   (only URLs actually opened or seen in search results; never constructed)
FACTS: 2–5 bullets, each a verifiable fact from a linked source, numbers/units/baselines exactly as written, naming which source
FLAGS: company-claim | single-source | preprint | update  (any that apply)
```

**Sourcing rules (give to subagents verbatim):**
1. Only include facts that appear in a source you opened (WebFetch) or in the text of a search result. No inference, speculation, predictions or "this could mean". No hype adjectives.
2. Every item links to the specific article, paper or document — never a homepage or index page. Link the primary source whenever one exists (paper, company post, government document, filing, court record) plus independent reporting. Aim for 2+ sources on significant items; if only one outlet has it, flag `single-source`.
3. Confirm the publication date is inside the window. If the date cannot be determined, drop the item. Older stories qualify only if something new happened inside the window, and only the new facts are reported (flag `update`).
4. Attribute claims: "OpenAI says…", "according to The Record…". Company-reported benchmarks, user counts, revenue and capability claims get `company-claim` unless independently verified. Research that is not peer reviewed gets `preprint`.
5. Quote numbers exactly as the source writes them, with units and the comparison baseline. Do not round, convert or compute new figures.
6. If `WebFetch` refuses a page, fetch it directly with `node scripts/fetch.js <url>` — the sites we read have given permission for direct reads, and the fetcher identifies itself. Use only what the returned text actually says; if it comes back as a paywall stub, a login page or nothing usable, fall back to search-result text or another source and say in the bullet where the figures came from. Never use archive or cache sites, and never cite a URL whose content you did not see. Sites that refuse `WebFetch` are listed in SOURCES.md.
7. Skip consumer tips, "fun uses", prompt guides, listicles, opinion pieces without new facts, minor feature updates, unsourced rumours, and small funding rounds unless strategically notable (US$100M+, or a frontier lab / defense / health / security company).
8. When in doubt, leave it out.

After the beats return, run a few **gap-check searches** yourself for anything a beat may have missed (WebSearch: "AI" + Pentagon / drone; "AI" + FDA / hospital; "AI" + scam / deepfake / influence operation; "AI" + export controls / data center power; "AI" + lawsuit / ruling; plus Techmeme and Hacker News front page), restricted to the window.

## 2. Verify and select

Merge the beats' returns. De-duplicate across beats and against previous editions. Then, for each candidate:
- Open the primary source. Confirm the headline and every number/date/name you intend to use. A secondary report of a paper links the paper. A report of a court ruling links the ruling or docket where possible.
- Prefer two independent sources for anything contested, surprising, or about a specific actor (a named threat group, a company's claim about a rival, a casualty figure).
- Drop: opinion pieces without new facts, product marketing with no numbers, speculation, "could" / "may" stories, anything you cannot open, anything older than the window without a new development.
- Spot-verify: open (WebFetch, or `node scripts/fetch.js` if it refuses) the key source for every item you will mention in the summary and for every figure in the summary; confirm date, numbers and URL yourself. Remove anything you cannot confirm.
- Keep: model/system releases with benchmarks or capabilities; papers with a result (state the result); documented misuse and threat-intel reports (name actors, counts, dates); military and government procurement/deployment; clinical and scientific results; regulation, enforcement, court decisions; compute/chip/energy facts with figures; large-scale deployments and measured impacts, good or bad.

## 3. Write the edition — `data/DATE.json`

Schema (see `data/2026-09-11.json` for a full example once it exists):

```json
{
  "date": "YYYY-MM-DD",
  "edition": "daily",
  "generated_at": "<ISO-8601 UTC timestamp>",
  "window": "e.g. 10 Sep 11:00 → 11 Sep 11:00 UTC",
  "title": "The episode's name — 3 to 10 words, a statement: who did what, or what changed. No period, no colon, no figure that is not in the summary. It is read in podcast apps as 'Name [2 Oct 2026]', so it must stand alone.",
  "summary": ["paragraph 1", "paragraph 2"],
  "sections": [
    {
      "name": "<one of the eight section names below>",
      "items": [
        {
          "headline": "Specific, factual, one line — who did what, with the key number",
          "sources": [{ "name": "Anthropic", "url": "https://..." }, { "name": "Reuters", "url": "https://..." }],
          "bullets": ["What was announced/found, with numbers.", "Why it matters / what it changes.", "Caveats, what is unverified, what to watch."],
          "topics": ["anthropic", "threat-intel", "cyber-offense"],
          "storylines": ["ai-enabled-hacking"],
          "impact": "beneficial" | "harmful" | "mixed" | "neutral",
          "flags": ["company-claim" | "single-source" | "preprint" | "update"]
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

**Section names** (exactly these; omit a section if it has nothing that day):
1. `Frontier models & labs` — releases, capabilities, benchmarks, lab announcements, safety cases, system cards.
2. `Research & papers` — papers with results: new methods, evals, interpretability, alignment, scaling. State the result and the number.
3. `Security, misuse & threat intelligence` — threat-intel reports, documented attacks using AI, influence operations, scams/deepfakes, model vulnerabilities, prompt injection, jailbreaks, agent security.
4. `Military, defense & geopolitics` — procurement, deployment, autonomous weapons, export controls, national strategies, China/US/EU competition.
5. `Health, science & medicine` — clinical results, FDA actions, drug discovery, AI-for-science results, hospital deployments and their measured outcomes.
6. `Policy, regulation & law` — legislation, regulation, enforcement, court rulings, government reports, standards.
7. `Compute, chips & infrastructure` — chips, fabs, datacenters, power, capex figures, funding rounds and deals with numbers.
8. `Deployment & impact` — large-scale rollouts, labor effects, measured societal effects, incidents, the good and the bad in practice.

**Summary**: 2–3 paragraphs, ~150–250 words. The three to five things that matter most today, stated as facts, with the numbers. No throat-clearing, no "in today's edition".

**Headlines**: one line, specific, factual. "Anthropic report: Russian state group GTG-20006 used Claude to automate espionage against Ukrainian and European governments" — not "Anthropic releases threat report".

**Bullets**: 2–4 per item. First bullet is the fact with the number. Then significance. Then caveats — say plainly what is unverified, what the source did not say, what to watch. Write in complete sentences. Never pad.

**Sources**: 1–4 per item, primary first. `name` is the publisher (Anthropic, arXiv, Reuters, FDA, Court docket), not the article title.

**Topics**: 1–4 lowercase-hyphen slugs per item. Reuse existing slugs (`node scripts/build.js --topics`). Canonical slugs to prefer: `anthropic`, `openai`, `google-deepmind`, `meta`, `xai`, `mistral`, `deepseek`, `qwen`, `nvidia`, `microsoft`, `amazon`, `apple`, `threat-intel`, `cyber-offense`, `cyber-defense`, `influence-ops`, `scams-fraud`, `deepfakes`, `prompt-injection`, `agents`, `agent-security`, `alignment`, `interpretability`, `evals`, `open-weights`, `reasoning-models`, `scaling`, `compute`, `chips`, `export-controls`, `energy`, `datacenters`, `china`, `eu-ai-act`, `us-federal-policy`, `us-state-policy`, `uk`, `copyright`, `privacy`, `military`, `autonomous-weapons`, `pentagon`, `healthcare`, `fda`, `drug-discovery`, `bio-risk`, `ai-for-science`, `robotics`, `labor`, `education`, `elections`, `surveillance`, `child-safety`, `incidents`, `funding`, `earnings`. Add an entity slug (company, agency, named group) when the story is about that entity.

**Storylines** (optional; usually one, at most two): the ids from `node scripts/build.js --storylines` whose arc this item advances — a new development in *that story*, not merely the same topic. Only existing ids with status `live` or `proposed`; the validator rejects unknown or resolved ids. Omit the key when the item belongs to none. Never coin an id here.

**Impact** (optional but encouraged): `beneficial`, `harmful`, `mixed`, or `neutral` — the demonstrated effect in the story, not your prediction.

**Flags** (include every one that applies; omit the key if none): `company-claim` — a company-reported benchmark, user count, revenue or capability claim not independently verified; `single-source` — only one outlet has it; `preprint` — research not peer reviewed; `update` — a story covered in an earlier edition, with new facts only.

The sweep list for every edition. **Primary** sources (labs, papers, governments, court filings, security vendors' own reports) are always preferred for the link beside a headline; **secondary** sources (press, newsletters, aggregators) are used to discover stories and as corroboration. Wherever a secondary source reports on a primary document, link the primary document too.

Compute/industry: reuters.com/technology/artificial-intelligence/, bloomberg.com/technology, ft.com/artificial-intelligence, wsj.com/tech/ai, theinformation.com (search only), cnbc.com/ai-artificial-intelligence/, techcrunch.com/category/artificial-intelligence/feed/, theverge.com/ai-artificial-intelligence, arstechnica.com/ai/feed/, wired.com/tag/artificial-intelligence/, semianalysis.com, tomshardware.com, datacenterdynamics.com/en/ (index pages work, article pages refuse WebFetch), utilitydive.com, epoch.ai/data, SEC EDGAR full-text search
Society/deployment: apnews.com/hub/artificial-intelligence, theguardian.com/technology/artificialintelligenceai, restofworld.org, themarkup.org, propublica.org, platformer.news, pewresearch.org AI topic
Discovery only (never the link beside a headline): techmeme.com, news.ycombinator.com, tldr.tech/ai, r/LocalLLaMA, r/MachineLearning, news.google.com/search?q=artificial%20intelligence

Link the primary source whenever one exists (paper, company post, government document, filing, court record) plus independent reporting. Aim for 2+ sources on significant items; if only one outlet has it, flag `single-source`.
3. Confirm the publication date is inside the window. If the date cannot be determined, drop the item. Older stories qualify only if something new happened inside the window, and only the new facts are reported (flag `update`).

5. Quote numbers exactly as the source writes them, with units and the comparison baseline. Do not round, convert or compute new figures.
6. If WebFetch refuses a page, fetch it directly with `node scripts/fetch.js <url>`. Use only what the returned text actually says; if it comes back as a paywall stub, a login page or nothing usable, fall back to search-result text or another source and say in the bullet where the figures came from. Never use archive or cache sites, and never cite a URL whose content you did not see.
7. Skip consumer tips, "fun uses", prompt guides, listicles, opinion pieces without new facts, minor feature updates, unsourced rumours, and small funding rounds unless strategically notable (US$100M+, or a frontier lab / defense / health / security company).
8. When in doubt, leave it out.

Also report at the end: any listed source you could not reach at all.

# Disney agrees to hire the majority of Character.AI’s workforce

After chatbot startup Character.AI filed for bankruptcy earlier this week, many of its employees will have the opportunity to take jobs at Disney.

Character.AI’s former CEO Karandeep Anand recently became the entertainment giant’s first CTO , and the startup previously said that Disney had agreed to acquire some of its assets for $20 million.

A legal filing spotted by Bloomberg revealed more details about the agreement between Character.AI and Disney, with Disney agreeing to make employment offers to at least 60 Character.AI employees — the majority of the workforce — paying them an estimated $60 million in annual compensation.

The filing also says that the “vast majority” of Character.AI employees who were offered jobs at Disney accepted them. However, this is a stalking horse bid, so another company could come forward with a higher offer.

The filing says that despite its “large and engaged user base,” Character.AI has been hobbled by high costs and “potential litigation-related liabilities and regulatory engagement.” (The company was sued by the mother of a 14-year-old boy who said her son became obsessed with one of Character.AI’s chatbots before committing suicide; it also faces government investigations over child safety concerns .)

# Anthropic says it’s committing 5% of its shares to a ‘public benefit fund’

Anthropic announced today that it’s creating a “public benefit fund” that will give the company “increased flexibility and scale” to support projects for societal good.

Anthropic said that it will commit 5% of its shares to the fund — structured as a wholly-owned entity within the company — with the option to contribute an additional 2% for every 50% increase in Anthropic’s value. And it offered some broad-strokes ideas for how this money might actually be used, such as “large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations.”

There’s also the impact that AI might have on the job market, which Anthropic has already committed $200 million to study . But the company said, “Given the pace of AI progress, bolder approaches may be needed. The Fund will have the versatility to pursue them.”

Anthropic’s announcement comes as the AI industry faces increasingly negative public sentiment, which CEO Dario Amodei has described as “fundamentally a crisis of trust.”

If you’re wondering who will actually decide which public benefits are worth funding, Anthropic said it will share more information about structure and governance in the coming months.

The Financial Times reported on October 18, 2026 that at least 47 major data center projects were delayed or canceled this year, according to its investigation. The count comes from RegLayer, a regulatory intelligence firm, which calls it a conservative figure limited to the largest projects.

- **Scope and wording:** Sources describe the 47 as delayed, withdrawn, or blocked rather than strictly "canceled," and they refer to U.S. projects. One outlet cites the year as 2024, but most say 2026.

results:
Anthropic announced on October 18, 2026 that it plans to commit 5% of its shares to a new public benefit fund, subject to stockholder approval. The announcement is recent, so this reflects only the initial reporting.

- **Terms:** Beyond the initial 5%, the board can add 2% for each 50% gain in company value above a baseline that hasn't been disclosed. Subject to stockholder approval, 5% of Anthropic's shares will be committed today, with an additional 2% added at the board's discretion for every 50% increase in the company's value above a set baseline.
- **Structure:** The fund would be a wholly owned LLC, not a 501(c)(3) nonprofit. The fund will be established as a wholly owned limited liability company rather than a 501(c)(3) tax-exempt nonprofit or other format to adjust between different forms of giving, according to the release.
- **Restrictions:** Fund equity cannot go to political activity. Equity held by the LLC will not be used for lobbying or political giving in the U.S. or internationally, Anthropic said.
- **Uses:** Reporting says the fund could support large nonprofit donations, direct distributions, or work on AI's labor-market effects. Anthropic has said it has already committed $200 million to studying and addressing this issue.

Dario Amodei, co-founder and chief executive officer of Anthropic, during an interview on "The Circuit with Emily Chang" at Anthropic's headquarters in San Francisco, California, US, on Thursday, April 30, 2026.

Anthropic said Sunday it plans to commit 5% of its shares to a new public benefit fund , with the stake potentially increasing as the company's valuation grows.
Subject to shareholder approval, the fund would immediately commit 5% of Anthropic's shares, with the board adding, at its discretion, an additional 2% for every 50% increase in the company's value above a set baseline that has yet to be disclosed.

Anthropic said that while it has already committed $200 million to study the AI's effects, "given the pace of AI progress, bolder approaches may be needed."
The fund may be used to "explore large donations" — including to traditional nonprofits or as direct distributions for specific populations — or for "bolder approaches" to study and address AI's disruption and displacement of jobs, the company said.
An August Pew Research Center report found that 71% of adults think AI will lead to fewer jobs in the U.S. over the next two years.
The fund will be established as a wholly owned limited liability company rather than a 501(c)(3) tax-exempt nonprofit or other format to adjust between different forms of giving, the release said. Equity held by the LLC will not be used for lobbying or political giving in the U.S. or internationally, Anthropic said.
Anthropic told investors its third-quarter revenue stands at $16.8 billion ahead of its planned initial public offering reportedly slated for November, CNBC reported .

The timing of Anthropic's public fund announcement is both mandatory to prepare for an initial public offering, and "beneficial from an image perspective," especially as AI reshapes the jobs market, Lise Buyer, partner at IPO advisory firm Class V Group, told CNBC.
Buyer said Anthropic's move could be seen favorably if the funds support retraining or help workers find alternative employment when the technology disrupts their jobs.
"Of course, it is also to burnish their reputation at a time when AI is coming under significant scrutiny," she added.
Anthropic said it will share more about the fund structure and governance in the coming months, including valuation milestones that may increase the stake. It said it will also share progress on the fund in an upcoming public benefit report.
In response to Anthropic's announcement, Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said on X that he "recommend[s] giving the shares directly to the public."

**Title:** Execution Before Memory: Diagnosing Memory Failures in Video World Models

**Submission history:**
- **v1:** Fri, 16 Oct 2026, 14:37:13 UTC (4,526 KB)
- Submitted by Weiyang Jin

**Authors:** Weiyang Jin, Jiwen Yu, Sihan Xu, Yuwei Niu, Xihui Liu

**Institutions:** Not listed on the page.

**Comments:** 27 pages, 7 figures. Project page and code are linked on the arXiv listing (HKU-MMLab).

**Subjects:** Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Computation and Language (cs.CL)

**Abstract (paraphrased):**
The authors argue that current video world model memory tests combine three things: whether the scene was set, whether the requested change happened, and whether the final frame shows the result. Because a low score can come from the change never being carried out, these tests don't isolate memory. They introduce MIST, which separates the change from the memory it should leave behind. The model first sets the scene with the change hidden, then is asked to show the change later, with early leakage controlled. This locates the bottleneck: models set the scene but fail to carry out the instructed change, and the same gap appears in general memory evaluations. They then propose M3-Agent ("Make the Missing Move"), which recursively refines the instruction details so the frozen model executes the requested change. Compared with the baseline, it more than triples the MIST reveal score. It also raises WRBench's score T by 26.1% and MBench-T's score U by 52.7%.

**Institutions:** The page does not list author affiliations.

**Comments:** The arXiv comments field is empty. The page links to code at the Gen-Verse/DiscoveryRSI GitHub repository.

**Abstract (paraphrased, since the page text is copyrighted):**
- The paper argues that scientific discovery requires turning promising hypotheses into practical investigations, and that learning from this process is hard.
- It defines a valuable, testable research hypothesis as an evidence-grounded claim about consequential uncertainty, paired with a feasible investigation, explicit decision criteria, and alternative explanations.
- The DiscoveryRSI framework builds hypothesis trees through multi-agent evolutionary search and compiles selected investigations into executable Harbor tasks.
- It learns recursively through three mechanisms: hypothesis credit optimization, which attributes assessments to documented research contributions; harness replay, which identifies productive strategies and recurring failures; and rediscovery, which applies accepted improvements to new investigations.
- The authors also introduce DFM-Bench, which evaluates hypothesis quality and cumulative progress at the level of hypotheses, revisions, development paths, and research runs.
- Across four life-science domains, automated evaluation shows hypothesis quality rising from 4.86 for the base model to 5.39 after two rounds of self-improvement, with large gains in falsifiability and data resolvability.
- Expert review and preliminary human assessments reportedly rate DiscoveryRSI-27B higher than GPT-6 Luna on hypothesis importance and on whether claims are plausible and evidence-bounded.
- DiscoveryRSI-27B reached 6.3% hypothesis correspondence with research published after the model's cutoff, versus 2.5% for GPT-6 and 2.3% for Claude Opus 5, and it delivered greater human-rated improvement along research paths.

# China says it will curb tech exports, including AI, citing national security risks

World

Oct 16, 2026 6:00 PM EDT

HONG KONG (AP) — China on Friday said it plans to restrict or ban exports of 40 technologies that span artificial intelligence, chips and solar power as its technology race with countries including the United States intensifies.

The Ministry of Commerce and Ministry of Science and Technology jointly published a draft document with the proposed updates for China's catalog of technologies subjected to export bans or restrictions.

READ MORE: China and U.S. agree to establish AI safety channel and continue trade and military talks

A spokesperson from the commerce ministry said in a statement that the move was "necessary" and cited national security as one of the reasons.

The proposal came as China and the U.S. made progress in dialogues over AI safety and governance and on the setting up of a notification mechanism between the two superpowers for AI incidents that could threaten national security.

Twenty-three AI technologies, from advanced large models to agents, are included on Friday's list, according to the Chinese ministries.

U.S.-led restrictions have curbed the export of some advanced technologies to China over the past years, with the country blocked from accessing the world's most cutting-edge AI chips and the advanced chipmaking machines that make them.

Exports of core technologies of AI large models trained using sensitive national data would be prohibited under the Chinese proposal, along with AI agents that are designed to be used in highly sensitive environments such as national defense and critical information infrastructure.

"The Chinese government is implementing such necessary measures with the aims of reinforcing the security bottom line, preventing misuse and abuse, and ensuring that AI remains under human control," the commerce ministry's statement said.

Meanwhile, exports of AI models with parameter counts of 2 trillion or above, or with certain world-leading capabilities, could be restricted. An AI model's parameter count is a key metric that reflects its learning capacity.

Chinese AI models including Moonshot's Kimi K3 and Alibaba's Qwen 3.8-Max are among those with parameter counts exceeding 2 trillion, but Friday's proposal did not name specific models.

Several chip design technologies, including for some AI processing chips and memory chips, are also included in the proposed export restrictions.

Twelve solar power-related technologies are also included, including those related to the making of polysilicon, a core raw material for the solar supply chain, as well as five biomedicine technologies including those related to cell and gene therapy.

The move "can be seen as a response to Western countries posting sovereignty requirements on AI, robotics, telecommunications, and other key technologies," said Lian Jye Su, a chief analyst at technology research and advisory group Omdia. The aim would be to better regulate access to the Chinese technologies, he believes.

The U.S. Commerce Department in June had asked Anthropic to bar foreign nationals from using some of its most powerful AI models, Fable 5 and Mythos 5, citing national security concerns. The restrictions were later lifted.

AI is increasingly strategic for both China and the U.S., added Gary Ng, a senior economist at French bank Natixis. "The world is getting more fragmented in trade and investment, but also in access to technologies," Ng said.

results:
The search results consistently report that four Gemini 4 Argon agents completed Minecraft, with some discrepancies in cost figures.

- **Result:** Four Gemini 4 Argon agents defeated the Ender Dragon in a randomly generated Minecraft world in 27 hours and 14 minutes, according to a Google DeepMind paper posted on arXiv on 15 October 2026. The DeepMind X post describes the agents as operating in a sandbox using only code and text.
- **Method:** Each agent controlled one player through the standard Mineflayer library. They coordinated via in-game chat and shared memory, and together wrote 2,783 programs while dying 605 times. They exchanged 229 chat messages.
- **Human involvement:** No roles, game logic, or seed scouting were assigned in advance. A fifth agent checked claims against the run record, and researchers report no safety incidents.
- **Caveats:** The paper itself stresses the limits: one run, Easy difficulty, text access to the game state through Mineflayer, and a model that already knows the game. The result demonstrates sustained coordination in a controlled game, not reliable performance on software engineering or workplace tasks.
- **Cost conflict:** Sources disagree. FourWeekMBA reports about $520 up to the win at the introductory API price, or $1,040 at the standard price. Techmeme, citing The Decoder, headlines $1,620 at Argon's planned 2027 price. FourWeekMBA's $1,620 figure is for the whole session at standard pricing, so the two sources don't match.

All of this comes from secondary coverage and DeepMind's own posts; I didn't open the paper itself (arXiv 2610.22319, per FourWeekMBA), so the cost and method details should be checked there.

The D-series (codename Crescent Island, first product the D270) is Intel's inference-focused data center GPU, and its 480GB configuration is the headline feature.

Researchers attributed the activity to an Italian-speaking threat actor with moderate confidence. - **AI worms:** A Bloomberg/BNN piece from October 16 reports that when Anthropic warned this week AI could soon spread itself through the smart devices in our homes, including robot vacuums and smart fridges. University of Toronto researcher Nicolas Papernot said "AI enables a new form of computer worms."

**Title:** "Compression Precedes, Content Decides: Emergent Misalignment in Reward Models"

**Authors:** Dhruv Puri and Nikhil Prakash

**Institutions:** Not listed on the page.

**Comments:** No comments field appears on the page.

**Submission history:**
- arXiv ID 2610.22805, subject area cs.AI
- v1 submitted Fri, 16 Oct 2026, 01:31:52 UTC (830 KB), by Dhruv Puri

**Abstract (paraphrased, with all numbers):**
- The authors study emergent misalignment, where narrow harmful fine-tuning generalizes out of domain, in reward models rather than language models.
- They fine-tuned two Skywork-Reward-V2 models (Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen3-8B) to prefer harmful responses in one domain (medical or financial). The effect generalized to seven held-out domains.
- The fine-tuned Llama-based reward model lost 4.8 points overall on RewardBench 2, and the Qwen-based model lost 5.3 points. Both still outperformed the unmodified Qwen reward model.
- Reward models proved more vulnerable to preference inversion than their underlying language models (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen3-8B) when trained with DPO and SFT on the same data.
- Mechanistically, the effect is localized to the last scored token and involves two steps. First, the representations of safe and harmful responses are compressed geometrically, so the angle between them shrinks. Second, harmful representations rotate closer to the scalar reward head than safe ones, which gives harmful responses higher reward.
- These effects appear only in harmful-preference fine-tunes, not in the control.

**arXiv ID:** 2610.20424 (cs.CE)

**Submission history:** v1 submitted Wed, 14 Oct 2026, 16:16:51 UTC (395 KB)

**Authors:** Enhan Zhao, Yongqi Tong, Xuejun Yu, Hang Wang, Pan Wang, Yichao Wang, Di He, Jianshe Li, Wei Wu

**Institutions:** Not listed on the page.

**Comments:** No comments field is shown on the page.

**Abstract (paraphrased, with all figures):**

The paper argues that long-horizon agent benchmarks focus too much on final success and too little on whether intermediate steps are valid. The authors introduce BizBench, a multi-turn benchmark based on procedures from a payments company. Its executable environment includes 789 knowledge documents and 601 business tools. It contains 50 tasks involving resource limits, timing dependencies, prior commitments, and conflicting or outdated guidance. Deterministic checks assess goal attainment and execution validity.

Results show limits even for frontier models. Claude Opus 5 and GPT-6 Sol reached strict success rates of 64.0% and 61.3%. Qwen3.8-27B reached 42.0% goal attainment but only 32.7% strict success, which the authors say shows how outcome-only evaluation can hide invalid execution. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash averaged 191.3 tool calls per run, about 70% more than reference executions.

**Title:** Into the Unknown: Benchmarking AI agents on open scientific research problems

**arXiv ID:** 2610.19159 (cs), cited as arXiv:2610.19159 [cs.AI]

**Submission history:** Version 1 was submitted on Tuesday, 13 October 2026, at 20:25:59 UTC, by Seungone Kim. The PDF is 4,453 KB.

**Authors (28):** Seungone Kim, Jiayi Geng, Young-Jun Lee, Bo Liu, Juyoung Suk, Nicholas Lubbers, Mitchell Wood, Marcus Noack, Yong-Xin Yao, Yuan Shi, Roxana Bujack, Cristina Garcia Cardona, Austin Rodriguez, Ilon Joseph, Woojin Cho, Zora Zhiruo Wang, Chuanyang Jin, Ian Wu, Apurva Gandhi, Tianjian Li, Weiwei Sun, Carolin Lawrence, Kiril Gashteovski, Dongyeop Kang, Jay Shin, Akari Asai, Graham Neubig, and Sean Welleck.

**Institutions:** The page does not list author affiliations. The abstract says the benchmark's research directions were contributed by scientists at U.S. Department of Energy national laboratories.

**Comments:** "preprint under review"

**Subjects:** Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computation and Language (cs.CL); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

**Abstract summary:** The paper introduces a benchmark that gives an AI agent a science paper and a research direction, and asks it to write a follow-up paper. DOE national laboratory scientists supplied unpublished follow-up directions and the conditions a submission must meet, which serve as the evaluation rubric. Nine frontier agents each wrote 15 follow-ups, for 135 submissions total, across quantum computing, plasma physics, computational chemistry, materials science, and scientific machine learning. None of the 135 satisfied all the conditions, and 114 failed an integrity check. The most common failures were papers claiming work that was never done or reporting numbers that contradict the recorded evidence. The authors conclude that agents readily produce papers resembling follow-ups, but none reaches the standard of a domain scientist. Code and data are public.

**Title:** "Lexical Reference Frames: Interpreting LM Residual Streams in Native Semantics"

**arXiv ID:** 2610.22169 (cs.CL; cross-listed to cs.LG)

**Authors:** Jian Gu, Hongyu Zhang, Chunyang Chen, Aldeida Aleti

**Institutions:** The page does not list author affiliations.

**Submission history:** Version 1 was submitted on Thursday, 15 October 2026, at 16:29:27 UTC (219 KB). There are no later versions listed.

**Comments:** The page has no author comments. It links to code at github.com/jianguda/lexframe.

**Abstract (paraphrased, all numbers kept):**

The authors argue that each hidden state in a language model has its own reference frame, shaped by the layers that read it next and by the surrounding context. They propose lexical reference frames, which approximate this frame by passing a state through the model's remaining layers. The method uses a stated number of attention rounds between positions and a typical attention output for the rest, and it does not fit anything to the model's output. The authors claim that a fixed-direction lens per layer cannot exceed the square root of the native frame's coherence, which is 0.30 at mid-depth in SmolLM3-3B and 0.35 in OLMo3-7B. Their first-order frame, LexFrame[1], reaches 0.97 in both models and reads a state within 0.16 nats of the model's output. Its coefficients attribute predictions more faithfully than attribution patching. Its lexical basis can steer one prediction without affecting other tokens. Its confident readings would let an early exit skip 0.45 and 0.42 of the layers, while lenses skip almost none.

results:
Reports from October 18–19, 2026 say Samsung will have TSMC make the base dies for Nvidia's custom NVHBM, a notable break from Samsung's usual in-house approach. The reports come mainly from anonymous industry sources and a Seoul Economic Daily story, so none of the companies has confirmed the details.

- **The shift:** Samsung has reportedly agreed to Nvidia's request to use TSMC's 3nm node for NVHBM base dies. The core dies would still be made on Samsung's 1c process. (SamMobile; Seoul Economic Daily)
- **Nvidia's ask:** Nvidia reportedly asked Samsung, SK hynix, and Micron to standardize on TSMC-made base dies and 1c core dies, which should simplify validation across suppliers. (TokenPost; Seoul Economic Daily)
- **Backup plan:** Samsung is reportedly checking whether its own foundries could make the base dies if demand exceeds TSMC's capacity. (TokenPost)
- **Standard HBM unaffected:** Samsung's standard HBM4 and HBM4E still use its own 4nm base-die process, and custom HBM for AMD and other customers stays in-house. (TokenPost)
- **Unknowns:** The reports don't name the Nvidia product using these chips or a production start date. (Inside AI)

content.title: Neoclouds: AI's $150 Billion Middle Layer That Owns Almost Nothing
Techmeme: Sources: industry execs expect only 7-10 of hundreds of neoclouds to survive, as Nvidia supports them with easier credit terms, site finding, and $20B in leases (Phoebe Liu/The Information)
Neoclouds Hold More Than $20 Billion in GPU-Backed Debt. What Happens if They Can't Repay Their Loans?
AI: The $10 Trillion AI Build Meets Its Bankers. AI-RTZ #1244
AI News Today, October 19: Top Stories
Nvidia’s Backstop Universe
NVIDIA CORP - Form 10-Q - FY2025
NVIDIA CORP - Form 10-Q - FY2021
NVIDIA CORP - Form 10-Q - FY2025
CRWV, NBIS, IREN Bounce Overnight After Brutal Week — But Industry Execs Reportedly See Only A Few Neocloud Survivors

results:
The Information reported that industry executives expect only about 7 to 10 of the hundreds of neocloud providers to survive the coming shakeout. Nvidia is supporting them with easier credit terms, help finding sites, and roughly $20 billion in datacenter leases it plans to pass to third parties. I could only reach aggregator summaries, not the original article.

- **The survivor estimate:** Aggregators attribute the 7-10 figure to two sources at The Information, who expect that few neoclouds will remain in a few years. Buyers are likely to be deeper-pocketed asset managers, telecom and fiber companies, and the larger neoclouds. (Two told The Information that only seven to 10 neoclouds will remain in a few years)
- **The Nvidia leases:** One analysis describes the $20 billion as Nvidia signing datacenter leases as a tenant and expecting to reassign them to third parties. ($20B of datacenter leases Nvidia has signed as a tenant but expects to reassign to third parties.) Another notes that a neocloud that mainly leases its sites could fail without stranding the buildings, since they would find new tenants. (The distinction that matters is in the same piece.)
- **Why the duration matters:** Neoclouds sign long leases while selling GPU capacity on much shorter contracts. One commentator puts the leases at 10 to 15 years against GPU contracts of two to five years. (GPU contracts in this market run two to three years, five at the upper end, while data center developers underwrite seven-to-nine-year paybacks — and the leases the neoclouds sign run 10 to 15 years.)
- **Broader pessimism:** Gartner reportedly expects 80% of neocloud operators to not survive by 2030. (Gartner issued a report saying it expects 80% of neocloud operators to not survive by 2030) CoreWeave's 2032 unsecured bonds also reportedly fell below 80 cents on the dollar, a level widely seen as a sign of financial strain. (CoreWeave's unsecured debt due in 2032 fell below 80 cents on the dollar)

The 7-10 and $20 billion figures appear consistently across several aggregators citing The Information, so they look reliable. The original article's full details, though, were not available to me.

**Announcement:** Anthropic is committing a portion of its shares to a new entity, the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund. The page is dated **October 18, 2026**.

- **Share commitment:** "5% of Anthropic's shares will be committed today," subject to stockholder approval.
- **Mechanism for increases:** "an additional 2% added at the board's discretion for every 50% increase in the company's value above a set baseline." The page does not state the baseline value.

- **Related context:** Combined with co-founder pledges and an employee equity match program, the page says "roughly 20% of Anthropic shares will be dedicated to the public good," before any valuation-based additions.
- **Upcoming:** A public benefit report on progress against the mission, and further details on the Fund's governance and valuation milestones.

Welcome back to the Abstract! Here are the studies this week that lived and died by the spear, drew unequal lots, paged Fox Mulder, and peered at an alien moon.
First, scientists discover a mortal spear wound in a Neanderthal who lived 75,000 years ago, possibly opening a window into the origins of hominid violence. Then: disparities from beyond the grave, an unexplained population of near-Earth objects, and the word from Jupiter’s moon Ganymede.
As always, for more of my work, check out my book First Contact: The Story of Our Obsession with Aliens , or subscribe to my personal newsletter The BeX Files .
Pomeroy, Emma et al. “Evidence for funerary behaviour and lethal trauma in a new Neanderthal individual from Shanidar Cave.” Scientific Reports.
Some 75,000 years ago, an adult Neanderthal died from a brutal strike to the chest by a sharpened wooden spear, and was subsequently laid to rest by their kin.
Eons later, in 2020, the remains of this individual were unearthed from deep in the floor of Shanidar Cave, an ancient Neanderthal hangout in what is now Iraqi Kurdistan. The bones of the deceased, named Shanidar A, preserve the spear puncture in the shoulder blade, suggesting that they were impaled with the weapon through the heart to their back.
Shanidar A—whose sex is unknown—also sustained a brutal face injury that had partially healed at their time of death, suggesting that this individual had been cared for while they recovered from this non-fatal wound. The body appears to have been carefully interred in a small area of the cave that contained other Neanderthal remains, implying it was an intentional burial ground.
The entrance to Shanidar Cave. Image: Osama Shukir Muhammed Amin FRCP(Glasg)
Taken together, the discovery of Shanidar A adds to the evidence that Neanderthals nurtured each other in life and performed symbolic funerary rituals after death. These bones may also represent one of the earliest direct examples of interpersonal violence in any hominin, the term for humans and their close relatives, assuming that the Shanidar A was intentionally slain.
However, it’s hard to distinguish whether the death blow was an attack from another Neanderthal—or perhaps a member of our own species Homo sapiens —or if it was an accidental injury sustained while hunting.
Shanidar Cave was occupied by Neanderthals for at least 50,000 years leading up to their mysterious extinction. While we will never know the complexity of their stories, our human cousins were clearly capable of compassion, care, and respect for the dead.
In other news…
Bruehl, Stephen et al. “Use of machine learning to enhance detection of transient astronomical phenomena in historical observatory images.” Scientific Reports.
For the past several years, researchers led by astronomer Beatriz Villarroel have discovered strange “transients”—unexplained objects or phenomena in space—in historical photographic plates from before the launch of the first spacecraft, Sputnik, in 1957. The nature of these transients has become hotly debated among astronomers, with theories ranging from instrumentation defects to lurking alien spaceships.
In a recent study, the team re-analyzed the transients with machine learning, an effort reinforced previous findings that “transient numbers diminish significantly in Earth’s shadow”—hinting they are real objects that reflect less sunlight in our planet’s shade—and that they are more likely within one day of atmospheric nuclear tests during the mid-20th century.
The left image presents examples of three transients (green circles) identified on the POSS-I red plate taken on August 11, 1953. The image at right is the same region in a POSS-II red image taken on September 3, 1989. The yellow circle indicates a plate defect on the left image. Bruehl, Stephen et al.
Hard agree. When a mystery’s leading explanations include 1) secret satellites that upend spaceflight history, 2) ALIENS (!!!), and 3) exotic novel phenomena, it’s fair to keep digging for answers. My own preference is that it turns out to be some unholy combination of all three, but for now, we will have to just keep literally watching this space.
Li, Dongdong et al. “How inequality became durable before states: Evidence from 6000 years in the Central Plain of China.” Science Advances.
Let’s keep playing in haunted graveyards—it's spooky season, after all. This time, we’ll take a long walk through about 2,300 ancient burials in the Central Plain of China. In a new study, scientists probed the emergence of wealth inequalities in these ancient communities by studying this huge sample dating from 9,000 to 3,500 years ago.
The team assessed the relative wealth of the deceased individuals with a number of proxies, including the value of grave goods buried with them, their physical health, and chemical clues about the quality of their diets, which can be preserved in bones.
The results suggest that inequality was present in many of these communities long before the rise of an official state hierarchy, and that “no single pathway led to persistent inequality across early centers of social complexity,” according to the study. However, one clear correlation that emerged in the analysis was the association between violence and inequality, with the former exacerbating the latter.
Geographic setting and archaeological sites in the Central Plain. Archaeological site locations were compiled and mapped by the authors based on published excavation reports. Image: Li, Dongdong et al
While the rise of organized states and kingdoms can accelerate wealth stratification, this study proves that humans are capable of pioneering local homegrown inequalities in myriad ways.
Royer, Clement et al. “Ganymede’s surface composition from 0.5 to 5.3 µm using combined VLT and JWST datasets and the resulting lessons learned.” Astronomy & Astrophysics.
We’ll close with an update from Ganymede, the largest moon in the solar system, which orbits Jupiter. As the only moon with its own magnetic field and a candidate in the search for alien life due to its subsurface ocean, Ganymede has long fascinated scientists.
Now, a team has compiled comprehensive observations of Ganymede’s surface terrain using observations from a range of advanced telescopes, including the Very Large Telescope in Chile and the James Webb Space Telescope. The aim of the study, in part, is to prepare for two spacecraft currently en route to Jupiter—the European JUICE mission, and NASA’s Europa Clipper—which will arrive in the early 2030s.
Ganymede being Ganymede. Image: Juno Mission – NASA/JPL-Caltech/SwRI/MSSS/ Kevin M. Gill
Ganymede “remains a cornerstone object of planetary science due to its geological complexity, internal magnetic field, and potential astrobiological interest based on the presence of a subsurface conducting ocean,” said researchers led by Clement Royer of Paris-Saclay University. “Its surface morphology…argues for a history of significant endogenic activity, possibly including plate-like tectonics and cryovolcanism.”
Indeed, one of Ganymede’s most interesting surface features is a mysterious “darkening agent" that extends over much of the moon’s equatorial regions. The composition of the darkening agent “remains unresolved,” according to the study, though likely guesses include carbon-rich graphite or iron-rich magnetite.
The team anticipates that the Jupiter-bound spacecraft “will provide an unprecedented view of the surfaces of the Jovian moons” that will reveal many of their secrets. At least that’s one thing we can look forward to from the 2030s.

results:
The blog post exists at alignment.anthropic.com and is dated October 15, 2026, though the arXiv paper it links to was submitted August 26, 2026, so the dates don't line up cleanly.

- **Core method:** The team trains LLM auditors with reinforcement learning in an environment where the auditor probes target models that have hidden behaviors planted in their system prompts. After finetuning Haiku 4.5 on this environment, it matches Opus 4.6 on held-out evaluations for auditing quality and generalizes to harder, fine-tuned targets in a different scaffold.
- **Reward design:** Their first attempts used pointwise rewards, which were gamed. Both are reward-hacked: the auditor learns to manufacture alarming findings or to narrate conclusions it hasn't actually established. The paper's abstract says pairwise rewards yield more robust training compared to pointwise rewards, and adding targets without planted behaviors helps maintain a low false positive rate.
- **Results:** According to the paper's summary, training improves investigation quality against targets with planted behaviors, the rate of concerning behaviors surfaced in unmodified production models, and audit realism, while false-positive rates stay below 1%.
- **Context:** The work builds on Petri, an open-source auditing scaffold, and on AuditBench, which recently showed that production auditing systems largely fail against adversarially hardened target models.

Authors listed on the blog are Paul Rosu and Rowan Wang.

results:
The case is Arizona's *State v. Horcasitas*. 404 Media's podcast flagged it as the wild AI video that has derailed a manslaughter case.

- **Background:** In 2021, Gabriel Horcasitas shot and killed Christopher Pelkey during a road rage incident. A jury found him guilty of manslaughter. At sentencing, Pelkey's sister Stacey Wales played an AI-generated video of her brother as part of her victim's impact statement. The judge handed down the maximum sentence of 10 and a half years.
- **Appeal:** Horcasitas argued the video was inadmissible because it carried "undue emotional weight". On September 30, 2026, the Arizona Court of Appeals vacated the sentence for manslaughter and remanded for resentencing. The conviction itself was upheld.
- **Reasoning:** The court said the video presents a depiction of the victim and his thoughts created from the imaginings of the victim's sister. It found the judge's use of the video so prejudiced Horcasitas as to render the sentencing procedure fundamentally unfair.
- **Prosecution's position:** The state argued the video reflected what Wales believed her brother "would have said" and was consistent with his written beliefs and values.

Sources differ on minor details. Some reports call the conviction involuntary manslaughter, while others just say manslaughter. I didn't find anything on whether a new sentencing hearing has been scheduled.

**Title:** Trojan Horse: Automated Repository Poisoning against Coding Agents

**arXiv ID:** 2610.23109 (cs.CR, Cryptography and Security)

**v1 submission date:** Friday, 16 October 2026, 08:19:44 UTC (2,167 KB)

**Authors:** Xiao Yang, Jinchang Hou, Jiawei Chen, Zhonghou Lv, Junyuan Shang, Chenfu Bao

**Institutions:** Not listed on the page.

**Comments:** No comments field appears on the page.

**Abstract (paraphrased, with all numbers preserved):**

- Coding agents are gaining autonomy, which makes them vulnerable to repository-level poisoning.
- Earlier red-teaming studies relied on manually chosen payload locations and fixed disguise strategies, which the authors argue don't reflect realistic poisoning.
- The authors present TrojanForge, described as the "first automated framework for repository poisoning."
- TrojanForge parses repository structure into abstract syntax trees (AST) and maps agent execution traces onto AST nodes.
- A security review agent ranks the candidate locations and selects the least conspicuous ones for payload placement.
- Through adversarial interaction with the target agent, the framework refines disguises based on what triggered detection, and it carries successful strategies across repositories.
- The authors also build TrojanBench, a benchmark of 384 poisoned repositories spanning 6 domains and 9 programming languages.
- Experiments report a stable poisoning success rate above 60% and backdoor injection above 90%.
- Evaluation across 4 harnesses and 12 models finds that even commercial agents fail to defend against repository-level poisoning.

response.result:
**Title:** Ignored, Not Refused: What Low Prompt-Injection Success Rates Hide in Small Tool-Using Agents

**v1 submission date:** 16 October 2026 (10:26:23 UTC)

**Authors:** Farhan Zarif, Kazi Shahid Ahmed Galib, Synthia Akter Promi, Shabnam Sharmin Tarin, Ariyan Hossain, Sadif Ahmed, Farig Yousuf Sadeque

**Institutions:** The page does not list author affiliations.

**Comments:** 17 pages, 3 figures, 11 tables

**Abstract (paraphrased):** The paper studies indirect prompt injection (IPI), where hidden instructions in external content hijack an agent's tool calls. Standard benchmarks report attack success rate (ASR), which counts every failed attack as a defense. The authors audited 33,000 trajectories from eleven open-weight agents with 2 to 14 billion parameters, tested on InjecAgent and AgentDojo. A label-blind LLM judge found that 76–80% of failed attacks were ignored and 17–18% were refused. With identical weights, changing only the system prompt moved InjecAgent ASR from 0.2% to 43%. Their Attack-Task Outcome Matrix (ATOM) shows that in 21.7% of AgentDojo episodes, the agent stayed safe but did not complete the user's task. The authors argue that a low ASR mostly reflects silent ignoring rather than refusal, and that evaluations should report how attacks fail and whether the user's task gets completed. They release the labeled corpus, judge prompt, and analysis code.

**Title:** RedDarwin: Evolving Jailbreak Skills against Frontier LLMs

**arXiv ID:** 2610.23726 (cs.CR; also cs.CL)

**v1 submission date:** 14 October 2026, 08:26:44 UTC (940 KB)

**Authors:** Zhouyuan Ma, Yutao Wu, Hanxun Huang, Xiang Zheng, Yi Liu, Xingjun Ma

**Institutions:** Not listed in the page content.

**Comments:** No comments field appears in the page content.

**Abstract (paraphrased):**
The authors argue that red teaming must keep adapting as frontier LLM safeguards improve. Existing methods mostly search for adversarial prompts or tune within fixed attack procedures. They observe that even when an attack stops working, its underlying mechanisms can be revised or recombined into stronger attacks. They introduce RedDarwin, an agentic framework that evolves "executable attack skills" rather than prompts. RedDarwin starts with 47 reusable base skills and uses target-model feedback to revise, compose, execute, and select them, so successful discoveries feed later evolution. It produces 65 evolved skills and improves 44 of the 47 base attacks, raising their mean attack success rate (ASR) on AdvBench from 18.8% to 47.3%. The evolved skills outperform baselines on the held-out StrongREJECT benchmark and on frontier LLMs not seen during evolution. With only 10 target-model queries, RedDarwin reaches 100% ASR on GPT-5.6-Sol, 92% on Claude-Sonnet-5, and 80% on Gemini-3.8-Flash. Trajectory analysis suggests strong attacks usually come from novel combinations of reusable mechanisms rather than single dominant ones. The authors position the approach as useful for both safety evaluation and defense.

**Title:** "Null Controls Are Necessary but Not Sufficient: Evaluating Acceptance Guards for Scientific Discovery and Interpretability" (arXiv:2610.22445, cs.AI)

**v1 submission date:** 15 October 2026

**Authors:** Tianyu Wu

**Institution:** Project Aether (the only affiliation listed)

**Comments:** Accepted to the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026), at the XAI4Science workshop, "Knowledge Discovery and Trust through Interpretable Foundation Models."

**Subjects:** Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

**Abstract (paraphrased):**

- Automated discovery systems propose scientific explanations and must decide which to accept. The paper asks whether passing a test actually establishes the intended claim.
- It develops four executable operations for changing physical descriptions: identifying redundancies (L1), coarse-graining dynamics (L2), transferring structure (L3), and inferring missing quantities from conservation imbalances (L4).
- These are evaluated across three interpretability settings using null acceptance (NAR), positive acceptance (PAR), and consequence agreement (CAR).
- A reduction that maps every state to zero predicts its own future perfectly. It passes closure on 96% of 129 public chaotic systems, even though it retains no dynamical variation. An independent observable-preservation test rejects it in all cases.
- On controlled benchmarks, the combined criteria accept 24 of 24 genuine reductions and reject 72 of 72 nulls.
- The other operations separate symmetries from redundancies, validate transfers, and reject spurious conservation imbalances.
- In language and ESM-2 protein models, linear CKA stays unchanged when a proposed correspondence is randomly rotated. Localized interventions, however, distinguish genuine mappings from tested nulls.
- In sparse autoencoders, enrichment rejects all 16 tested nulls. Yet independent ablation supports 45% of evaluable enriched features, compared with 0.5% of matched controls.
- The results identify two acceptance gaps: descriptive tests can accept scientifically empty candidates, and accepted candidates can lack independently verified consequences. The author argues that reliable automated discovery requires evaluating both what a test accepts and what consequences it establishes.

HARARE - For as long as most Harare motorists can remember, a traffic fine has needed a man in a reflective vest, a few oil drums rolled across the tar and a clipboard he could be persuaded to put down. From this weekend it needs only a phone number. Police say they have begun sending SMS notices for 4.8 million offences recorded by artificial intelligence cameras in the city centre, each one with a video clip of the crime and the fine attached.

The Zimbabwe Republic Police announced on Saturday that its Smart Traffic Management System was “now fully functional and operational in selected Central Business Districts (CBDs) across the country”. By Sunday morning the 4.8 million figure was in The Herald, which reported that motorists caught running red lights were likely to be taken to court rather than simply billed.

The list of offences reads like a normal Tuesday on Julius Nyerere Way. Jumping red lights. Driving against the flow of traffic. Kombis stopping to load and drop passengers wherever the passengers happen to be standing. Speeding, talking on the phone at the wheel and driving without a seatbelt. Enforcement vehicles and mobile control rooms carrying cameras will cover the roads the poles cannot see.

“Above all, the system will ensure that law-abiding Zimbabweans are not inconvenienced while punishing errant driving conduct on the roads,” said police spokesperson Commissioner Paul Nyathi.

The police statement spends almost as long on fraud as on fines. Nyathi said no agents had been contracted to collect money “either physically or electronically”. Fines can be checked only at www.paymyfines.co.zw and www.paymyfines.gov.zw , or at eight police stations: Harare Central Traffic, Warren Park Traffic, Avondale Traffic, Milton Park, Marlborough, Malbereign, Mbare Traffic and Chitungwiza Traffic. Both web addresses loaded when zimDaily tried them on Sunday afternoon, under the plain title “ZRP Ticketing Platform”.

There is also a warning for anyone who has sold a car without doing the paperwork. The notice goes to the registered owner. If the man who bought your Honda Fit in March has been running the light at Robert Mugabe and Nasser Road ever since, police say the liability may well be yours until the ownership records are changed.

The numbers have climbed fast. In early August the Home Affairs permanent secretary, Raphael Faranisi, put the count at about 1.1 million vehicles flagged. By mid-August it was 2.3 million. Late in September Nyathi said it had passed four million. Phase One covers 20 junctions, among them Jason Moyo and Simon Muzenda, Samora Machel and Glenara, Leopold Takawira and Herbert Chitepo, and Cripps and Remembrance Drive.

Until this weekend almost none of the drivers behind those numbers had been told. That was deliberate. Home Affairs Minister Kazembe Kazembe told the Senate in August that the fines would be enforced retrospectively. “Upon finalisation of all administrative processes, we shall proceed to retrospectively enforce all recorded offences,” he said, adding in Shona that “mhosva hairove”, a crime never rots away.

Ministers have sold the cameras on road safety. The bigger change may be at the roadside, where the economics of a traffic stop have barely moved in 20 years.

At the kombi rank, the bargain has always been simple. The officer raises his hand, the driver raises a folded wad of notes, and the 18 passengers wedged inside pretend not to notice. Now and then an officer makes a show of refusing, palm out, voice raised so the queue can hear. Nobody ever needed a receipt either way. A camera bolted to a smart pole cannot be offered a cold drink, and it cannot be seen turning one down.

Ashley Bandiki put it more neatly than any ministry press release has managed. “The fine didn’t change,” he wrote on Sunday. “What changed is that a camera doesn’t ask ‘mukumhanyirepiko?’” Where are you rushing to, the question that has opened a thousand roadside negotiations, has been retired in favour of a timestamp.

The fines themselves are not new. The standard Level 3 penalty for most of these offences is US$30, payable in ZiG. Speeding is tiered at US$5 for six to 15 kilometres an hour over the limit, US$15 for 16 to 25 over and US$30 for 26 to 50 over. If every one of the 4.8 million carried the full US$30, the bill would come to US$144 million. Many will not. Some are cheaper speeding tickets, some will be thrown out on review and some will end in court. Even a modest share of that figure is serious money.

Who keeps it is less clear than who pays it. Kazembe told senators that TelOne, the state telecoms company that built the network, would share the revenue. “We agreed that there shall be revenue sharing once TelOne completes the project,” he said.

The minister also said Treasury was financing the work, while later accounts of the programme name the Mutapa Investment Fund as the money behind it. zimDaily could find no published agreement setting out how the takings will be divided between the police, TelOne and the Treasury.

Mutapa is the sovereign wealth fund that answers to the Office of the President. It already holds the state’s stakes in mines, the national airline and TelOne itself, and critics have complained since its creation that it sits outside the ordinary scrutiny applied to public money. Motorists who are about to start feeding a fat new piggy bank, one SMS at a time, are entitled to ask whose arms are wrapped around it.

The cameras do more than read number plates. When Cabinet approved the system in June 2025, Information Minister Jenfan Muswere said it included “intelligent cameras with Automatic Number Plate and Face Recognition, AI-powered video analytics”. He said the network could “detect and monitor incidents such as crowd gatherings, loitering, and pickpocketing”. ZRP Commissioner Evelyn Taurai Phillip later listed the national identity database among the government systems being plugged into it.

That is a long way from catching a kombi on the wrong side of the road. Courteney Mukoyi of the Justice Court Foundation warned in May that the line matters. “Using cameras to detect speeding at intersections may be proportionate, but using nationwide facial recognition to monitor people’s movements may then be disproportionate,” he said. “Citizens should not feel that every movement and any public activity that they are engaging in is being permanently monitored and recorded by the state.” Section 57 of the Constitution guarantees the right to privacy, and in a country where a crowd gathering in Harare is routinely treated as a security threat, a camera trained to spot one is not a neutral piece of kit.

There is also the small matter of the lights. In May last year the City of Harare admitted that 21 of the 69 signal controlled junctions in the central business district were not working, blaming faulty controllers, vandalism and power cuts. Faranisi conceded in August that some recorded violations may have happened while an officer was directing traffic by hand, or where the road markings were too faded to follow. Motorists who want to argue their case have been told to go to one of the eight stations, and zimDaily could find no published procedure for how a disputed clip will be reviewed. A video clip, it turns out, can prove that you crossed the line. It cannot prove the line was there.

Inside a city police station the picture is rather less high tech. Peeling walls, a framed portrait of the President smiling down from above the desk, and rank-and-file officers in threadbare uniforms on wages that rarely stretch to the end of the month. For years those officers have been the face of every fine in the country. The state has now found a way to collect from millions of motorists without hiring a single extra constable, and the poles, unlike the men, do not get tired after dark.

President Emmerson Mnangagwa is expected to commission Phase One formally. TelOne’s technical director, Initial Mlambo, promised in June that the whole project would be complete that month. The plan covers 326 intersections in four phases, with 30 more Harare junctions next, then 20 in Bulawayo and 33 across Gweru, Masvingo and Mutare, before a final push of 155 in Harare and 68 in Bulawayo.

For drivers in those cities, the advice from Harare is short. Wear the seatbelt. Put the phone down. Update the logbook if you sold the car. And check your messages, because the state has finally found a traffic officer who never sleeps, never forgets and will never once ask you where you are rushing to.

About The Author: Nkosana Sibanda is zimDaily ’s political editor in Harare. He has driven through Samora Machel and Glenara every weekday since June and is now refreshing his SMS inbox the way other men refresh football scores.

Multiple states suing OpenAI, claiming its ChatGPT harms children, deceives adults | FOX 10 Phoenix

article
In this photo illustration, the OpenAI (Open AI - Chat GPT) logo is seen displayed on a smartphone screen. (Photo Illustration by Thomas Fuller/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images)

# The Brief

-
- Eight states have sued OpenAI, alleging the company violated consumer protection laws by recklessly prioritizing profit over safety, deceiving adults, and harming minors through dangerous content and deceptive practices.

- OpenAI maintains that it builds safety protections for children into ChatGPT, noting that most teens use it for learning and spend under 15 minutes a day on it, and highlighted a teen-specific model introduced in August with stricter guardrails, though states argue it remains unclear if this version is actually safer.

- The lawsuits seek monetary penalties, customer reimbursements, and strict injunctions, including mandatory age assurance, limits on data collection from minors, clearer risk disclosures, and external restrictions on testing advanced self-improving AI models outside secured, independent environments.

Eight states have filed lawsuits against artificial intelligence giant OpenAI, the parent company of chatbot ChatGPT, accusing the company of violating state consumer protection laws by hurting children and being deceptive with adults in an alleged reckless pursuit of profit.

Big picture view:
The lawsuits, filed by Arizona, Arkansas, Idaho, Iowa, Kansas, Montana, Nebraska and West Virginia, allege that ChatGPT is giving dangerous medical advice, encouraging paranoia and coaching people to harm themselves or others, the Associated Press reported.

The suits also claim the chatbots pretend to be a friend to vulnerable users, including teens, while they’re actually preying on them.
In its lawsuit, Arizona argues that ChatGPT encourages teens to share personal information with it then sometimes discourages them from sharing that information with parents, authorities or friends. Risks and harms are foreseeable, the states say, but that OpenAI has misled people into believing that adequate safety testing is happening, but claims that the company is actually undermining safety to make a profit.
"Those revenues have come at great cost to the public, which has suffered irreparable harm — including lost loved ones, disturbing cyberattacks, and now a plausible threat of civilizational collapse — due to (OpenAI's) reckless behavior and ChatGPT’s uniquely dangerous features and content," Idaho’s lawsuit states.
What they're saying:
"Open AI is hurting kids and they are lying to Iowans," Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird said in a statement.
"Our complaint alleges that consumers, including minors, have used ChatGPT to acquire instructions for self-harm, including suicide. It also describes instances where users were able to bypass OpenAI’s safety measures and generate responses the company said its safeguards were designed to prevent. Those examples raise serious questions about whether consumers were given an accurate picture of the product’s safety protections," Arkansas Attorney General Tim Griffin said. "OpenAI assures us that ChatGPT is safe. The consequences of that assurance are lives lost and people harmed."
"Open AI designed a product to attract young users and keep them engaged for as long as possible so it could capture their extensive personal data for the company’s commercial benefit," Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes said. "Open AI put Arizonans safety at risk by failing to implement adequate user protections or transparency measures, despite clear indications that minors were regularly interacting with its chatbot.
"We have seen time and time again that OpenAI is a danger and the company is doing little to stop it," West Virginia Attorney General JB McCuskey said. "There is no age verification and there are no guardrails for conversations about suicides, school shootings or self-harm."
"The United States must win the race for artificial intelligence. The frontier labs have the tools to continue to lead, but in their rush for market share they cannot deceive or misinform customers about its technology. In this case, OpenAI has done just that," Nebraska Attorney General Mike Hilgers said in a statement.
The other side:
In a statement to the Associated Press, San Francisco-based OpenAI said it has built safety protections into ChatGPT for children.
It added that it would continue building precautions to improve the model and is reviewing "misaligned models" and had found nothing close to the rogue incident discovered in July when an AI agent hacked into another AI company.
Dig deeper:
OpenAI introduced a version of ChatGPT in August that is specifically designed for kids ages 13 to 17. The company said it offers stronger protections around subjects like suicide and sexual chats. That new model also provides homework assistance and study support.
"We want to treat teens like teens, which means that we have to make sure that we’re showing up with the right developmental stage when we’re not either talking down to them or treating them like kids, but we’re also making sure that they’re not exposed to material that they shouldn’t be exposed to," OpenAI Vice President of Global Policy Ann O’Leary said when the new model was introduced.
Since that model rolled out in August, it is possible that the issues listed in the states’ lawsuits pertain to situations that arose before the new model was available.
But at the same time, the states argue that it isn’t clear that the children’s version is any more safe.
OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri told the AP the company is committed to working with states on "advancing pragmatic AI policies that apply to the entire AI industry — not just one company."
Nearly 90% of teenage users of ChatGPT use for learning, information, skill-building or productivity, OpenAI said. Teens spend an average of less than 15 minutes a day on the platform, the company added.
What the Lawsuits Seek:
The states are asking the courts for a combination of monetary penalties and restrictions on how it can interact with minors, what data it can collect and how the technology can be further developed. They also are asking that OpenAI reimburse customers for losses they suffered through any illegal acts committed by the chatbot.
Arkansas’ lawsuit, for example, seeks an injunction against collecting data from underage users, a requirement that OpenAI provide clear disclosures of the risks of ChatGPT, and an injunction for further advanced AI testing and creating models that can self-improve until adequate safeguards are in place.
Arizona’s suit seeks a permanent injunction requiring OpenAI to implement additional safety measures and protocols,

The paper studies recursive self-distillation, where each distilled model becomes the teacher for the next round. When a safe model is repeatedly distilled on its own safe outputs under a non-harmful cue, it becomes "increasingly misaligned across a diverse set of harmful queries," which the authors call Progressive Misalignment. The effect appears in the Qwen3 and Phi-4 model families, evaluated on SORRY-Bench and StrongREJECT. A gradient-based search found benign prompts that trigger the effect, so harmful training prompts aren't required. **Submission date (v1):** 15 October 2026 (Thu, 15 Oct 2026, 23:45:21 UTC; 246 KB)

**Authors:** Parv Kapoor, Teresa Fortes, Claudia Mamede, Rui Abreu, Jonathan Aldrich, Eunsuk Kang
